subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Show that the locus of the feet of the perpendiculars drawn from either of the foci to any tangent to the ellipse is the auxiliary circle.

mark_split.label: Set up the tangent and the perpendicular from the focus
Solve the two equations for P

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2B (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.63 — SAQ chapter 8 Ellipse, answer 73. NOT on an SSP page. Printed appearances: AP 17,19. Book p.63 prints no margin mark tags for this proof-style question, so the 1+1+1+1 split here is OURS, following the four natural stages of the standard 'squaring and adding two equations' proof. A FIGURE is authored for this card — the ellipse, its auxiliary circle (same centre, radius a), one focus, a tangent line, and the foot of the perpendicular from the focus to that tangent — because the picture IS the argument here: seeing the foot of the perpendicular land on the circle is the entire content of the result. Ellipse is an SAQ-ONLY unit on the book's IPE Blue Print (book p.5). No two-book union check and no board back-test were possible for Maths-2B (no second-year TSBIE BLM on hand; the book's five Guess Papers pp.118-127 are the orchestrator's back-test stand-in).

insider_note: 'Squaring and adding' two equations that share the same two unknowns is the standard trick whenever a locus proof gives you a sum-of-squares condition like cos²θ + sin²θ = 1 to fall back on — the same trick as the director circle proof, applied differently.

steps.label: Set up the tangent and the perpendicular from the focus
steps.margin_note: First mark. The perpendicular from S(±ae, 0) to the tangent has slope −1/m.
steps.memory_tip: A line perpendicular to a slope-m line always has slope −1/m.
lines: Let the ellipse be S ≡ x²/a² + y²/b² − 1 = 0
Let P(x₁, y₁) be a point on the locus.
The perpendicular to this tangent through
steps.why: The foot of the perpendicular P is the point that lies on BOTH the tangent line and the perpendicular dropped from the focus onto it, so both lines' equations are written first, then solved together.
common_mistakes: Writing the perpendicular line through the centre instead of through the focus.
Using slope m for the perpendicular line instead of its negative reciprocal −1/m.

steps.label: Solve the two equations for P
steps.margin_note: Second mark. P(x₁, y₁) satisfies both (1) and (2), since it is their point of intersection.
steps.memory_tip: The foot of the perpendicular is exactly the intersection point of the two lines.
lines: P(x₁, y₁) is where (1) and (2) meet:
y₁ − mx₁ = ±√(a²m² + b²)  and  my₁ + x₁ = ±ae
steps.why: Since P lies on both lines by construction, its coordinates satisfy both equations simultaneously — this is what makes the next 'square and add' step possible.
common_mistakes: Solving each equation separately for m instead of keeping both as simultaneous conditions on P.
Losing the ± sign, which must stay consistent with the ± in step 1.

steps.label: Square and add
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Squaring each equation and adding eliminates m completely.
steps.memory_tip: Whenever two equations both equal ± something, squaring and adding removes the sign and often removes another unknown too.
steps.why: Squaring both equations before adding cancels the cross terms 2mx₁y₁ against each other, and replacing b² with a²(1 − e²) makes the right-hand side collapse to a single multiple of a².
common_mistakes: Forgetting to substitute b² = a²(1 − e²), which is what makes the a²e² and b² terms combine cleanly.
Missing that the two cross terms −2mx₁y₁ and +2mx₁y₁ cancel exactly when the equations are added.

steps.label: Conclude the locus
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. Both sides share the factor (1 + m²), which cancels.
steps.memory_tip: The auxiliary circle always has the SAME radius as the semi-major axis a.
lines: (x₁² + y₁²)(1 + m²) = a²(1 + m²) ⇒ x₁² + y₁² = a²

lines.text: Locus is x² + y² = a² — the auxiliary circle

steps.why: Cancelling the common factor (1 + m²) from both sides removes the slope m entirely, leaving x² + y² = a², the circle of radius a centred at the ellipse's own centre — the auxiliary circle.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to cancel (1 + m²), leaving m in the final answer, which cannot be a valid locus equation.
Naming the result the director circle instead of the auxiliary circle — the radius here is a, not √(a² + b²).

steps.label: The figure
steps.margin_note: No marks — the question does not ask for a diagram. Drawn because the picture IS the argument here.
steps.memory_tip: The auxiliary circle touches the ellipse at the two ends of the major axis.
steps.why: S is a focus, the slanted line is a tangent to the ellipse, and P is the foot of the perpendicular from S onto that tangent — P lands exactly on the auxiliary circle, which is what the proof shows algebraically.
common_mistakes: Drawing the perpendicular from the centre instead of from the focus S.
Drawing the circle the same size as the ellipse instead of touching it only at the ends of the major axis.
